En tant qu’immigrants, nous fréquentons: As immigrants, we frequent the businesses of our communities and use the products they offer to make a home of our lives in this part of the world. We make enormous efforts to adapt, but we also have to admit that there are things we miss. When you decide to start a new life, you leave a lot behind.
Voilà pourquoi, lorsqu’on trouve un endr: That is why finding a place that brings back a little piece of our old life feels like a gift. These establishments are part of our everyday lives. In a way, we adapt these products from our cultures to the lives we lead here, we introduce them to our children who are growing up here, and we give them a small piece of their identity, like one more piece of a big puzzle they will have to put together.
Ces commerces deviennent partie intégran: These businesses become an integral part of our routine, yet we know little about their founders, immigrants like us who arrived long ago and worked hard to start their lives over.
Je me suis intéressée à l’histoire du Se: I became interested in Señor José’s story because I know him as the official butcher of Montréal’s Latin American communities, but many of the things he told me surprised me. Among them, the fact that he arrived nearly 40 years ago, by way of Roxham Road, or that butchery was not his plan B, but the trade he had practised since a young age and managed to get back to. Some of what he revealed to me made me reflect on the fact that this kind of trade rests on a delicate equation and that, because of this, one day we may no longer have it.
J’espère que l’histoire de José sera une: I hope José’s story will be a source of inspiration for other people who come to take refuge in this city and are only beginning the enormous and difficult adventure of adapting. I also hope it will help show why our products and our traditions are more than mere culinary quirks, and that it will remind us why we must take care of them and preserve them.
<strong>Le boucher latino de Montréal, J: Montréal’s Latino butcher, José Rojas, is a well-known figure among meat lovers. Many customers, some travelling from very far away, come to him to get meat cut the same way as in their home countries. This is the story of a migration and nearly four decades devoted to this trade, and of its uncertain future.
Fin février, après une semaine de déplac: In late February, after a week of difficult travel, the sidewalks are completely covered in snow. Boucherie St-Viateur is quiet. A few customers come in, most of them regulars who greet each other by first name, in their respective languages: French, English, Spanish and Italian. There is something of a Tower of Babel of meat about the place.
Le propriétaire de la boucherie, José Ma: The owner of the butcher shop, José Manuel Rojas Acevedo, who is originally from Chile, is a true specialist in his field. Over his everyday clothes—jeans, a plaid shirt and a navy sweater—he puts on a white work apron and a black cap. His dark eyes are very lively, and almost every time he finishes a sentence, he does so with a smile. He welcomes customers from different parts of the island of Montréal and beyond. They come for the meat, but also and above all for the know-how: José is the only butcher who masters Latin American cuts. For many Latinos in general, meat is a cultural product in its own right.
« El señor José », comme l’appellent les: “El señor José,” as Montréal’s Hispanic community calls him, knows the difference between the cuts for an asado negro and an asado de tira, which meat to use to make hallacas or empanadas, how to flatten a milanesa to give it the ideal thickness and how to prepare Argentine-style chorizos. It may seem trivial, but for his customers, a good cut is not only a culinary matter; it touches on roots, family traditions, and even nostalgia for parents and grandparents who are no longer here.
Malgré la popularité de José, son histoi: Despite José’s popularity, his story is little known. His migration journey, made up of highs, lows and loops, began nearly 40 years ago.
<strong>La dimension méconnue du rêve ca: The little-known side of the Canadian dream
José a appris à préparer la viande dès l: José learned to prepare meat as a teenager, and he very quickly prospered.
« Avec mon beau-frère, j’ai commencé à t: “I started working with my brother-in-law, and then we opened a butcher shop in Santiago, Chile. Later, I was employed by a chain and I bought one of the branches, where I worked with my wife, Clara,” he explains from the other side of the counter.
Dans les années 1980, le Chili vivait so: In the 1980s, Chile was living under the dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet, a regime that repressed every form of dissent and is believed to have killed or disappeared more than 3,000 people, in addition to imprisoning and torturing tens of thousands of others. Some 200,000 Chilean citizens fled the country.
Cependant, ceux qui sont partis n’ont pa: However, not everyone who left emigrated because they were persecuted for political reasons. “Our situation wasn’t bad. Under the dictatorship there were ups and downs, it’s true, but acquaintances who had come to North America told us about how great it was and we thought we could make a lot of money. Of course, that wasn’t the case. It’s never the way they paint it for us. When you’re over there [in your country of origin], you can’t understand that when someone tells you, ‘I earn in dollars,’ every dollar earned is spent. I think it was greed; that’s the truth,” says José.
Sa découverte de Montréal a eu lieu il y: He discovered Montréal 39 years ago. He had come from the United States, after a nine-month stay in Boston with his brother-in-law, trying to achieve the American dream. But there, he never managed to fit in. He already saw himself going back to Chile when his brother-in-law confided that he planned to cross the border into Canada. José went to pick him up at the bus terminal, and his brother-in-law, in tears, asked him to come along. He did.
« Nous sommes montés dans un bus jusqu’à: “We took a bus to Plattsburgh [in New York State], and from there, we made the crossing” [via Roxham Road, closed since March 2023]. “A man drove us in a car and we got out five minutes before reaching the border. It was about midnight. He told us, ‘Cross over there and you’ll see some bikes. Take them, pedal for a quarter of an hour and I’ll pick you up on the other side.’” It was the fall of 1986.
Au Canada, sa vie commence dans une cham: In Canada, his life begins in a hotel room in downtown Montréal, with his brother-in-law as a companion and a cold that neither of them had ever known before.
<strong>Brûler ses navires pour s’assure: Burning your ships to make sure you move forward
Comme dans presque toutes les histoires: As in almost every migration story, the early days were very hard for José. Without a work permit, he could only find temporary jobs, paid in cash. “We managed to settle into a tiny apartment. We did anything, like delivering Publisacs. That allowed us to have enough money to pay the rent and to eat,” he says.
José, son beau-frère et sa sœur, qui est: José, his brother-in-law and his sister, who arrived later, benefited from Canada’s program for Chilean refugees. It was in effect from 1973 to 1989 and helped nearly 7,000 people. From 1979 to 1989, Quebec took in 3,379 Chileans, who settled mainly in Montréal.
« Il n’y avait pas beaucoup de travail i: “There wasn’t much work here. I thought about going back to the United States and returning to Chile, but I no longer had a passport.” Financial difficulties eventually caused friction within the family. Just a few months after they arrived, the brothers-in-law, who had been partners until then, fell out. José went to live with a friend. Soon after, that friend made an announcement that took him completely by surprise: “I talked to your wife. She told me she sold everything and she’s arriving tomorrow with the kids.”
Le 1<sup>er</sup> janvier 1987, Clara et: On January 1<sup>st</sup>, 1987, Clara and their two children, aged two and four, arrived in Canada. “We took an apartment, a 1½, and settled in with the things our friends gave us.”
Cette arrivée marque un changement décis: Her arrival marked a decisive change. Clara had sold everything they owned in Chile to pay for the trip. “We couldn’t go back. It was easier to start from scratch here,” he recalls. Since she spoke a little English, she found a job as a housekeeper for a family. The couple devoted themselves to learning French, he during the day, she in the evening, while the children worked hard at school to learn the language too. “A year went by before we realized it,” José remembers.
La sœur de José et son mari déménagent a: José’s sister and her husband then moved to Toronto. The family was permanently separated. “We found ourselves alone and, like all immigrants, we had to start from zero to make friends, to meet those people who end up becoming your children’s uncles and aunts, even though they aren’t family.” It was around this time that their third daughter was born. A year later, they received their work permit. Things then began to change for the better.
Grâce à l’expérience acquise au Chili, J: Thanks to the experience he had gained in Chile, José began working at a delicatessen in Montréal. He got in touch with Aldo, an Italian immigrant who owned a butcher shop. He worked a few shifts there and extended his hours until he became a full-time employee at Boucherie St-Viateur, located on the street of the same name.
La plupart des clients sont des Italiens: Most of the customers were Italians and Argentines, who liked dealing with José. Besides being a quick learner, he had a unique skill: he knew how to cut meat for South American customers.
En un clin d’œil, 16 ans se sont écoulés: In the blink of an eye, 16 years went by, during which the butcher shop moved to Saint-Laurent and Aldo offered José a partnership. They worked together for more than a decade, then the wheel of fortune turned again: “My partner won at Loto Québec and told me he wanted to sell his share of the business.” José jumped at the opportunity. “I found myself all alone and I moved here,” to the shop on Beaubien Street, in Little Italy, where he has been behind the counter for about fifteen years.
José est fier d’avoir su fidéliser une c: José is proud of having built a loyal clientele that admires him. “These are people from everywhere: Latinos, Italians, Quebecers.” He has watched a generation of customers grow up. “The older ones are gone, and now their children come for the Sunday asado or chorizo that reminds them of their parents,” he says in a nostalgic tone.
Nicolás est l’un de ces clients. « Tout: Nicolás is one of those customers. “Everybody knows José, he’s really warm. I remember when I was little, my dad found out there was someone who cut meat the Argentine way,” and the family started going to Boucherie St-Viateur. “Even today, it’s the butcher shop where all the Argentines go, and everyone who likes to eat meat the way they do back home.”
Les nouveaux immigrants arrivent grâce a: New immigrants arrive by word of mouth. Like Luis, a Venezuelan who lives in Saint-Hubert and comes to Montréal every month to get cuts like punta trasera for his barbecues. “I had lost the habit of buying meat the way it’s done in my country. I’d go to any chain and buy a tray, but it wasn’t the same. You have to talk to the butcher. The quality of the meat José sells is exceptional. You put it on the barbecue with a little salt, and that’s it,” he says.
L’entreprise de José se porte toujours b: José’s business is still doing well. But the future isn’t shaping up the way he would have wished: he is the last butcher in his line. A tragedy turned everything upside down.
Il y a huit ans, alors que lui et sa fem: Eight years ago, while he and his wife were on vacation in Chile, his youngest daughter died. She was only 27. “They called us to tell us and we came home right away. It’s the hardest trip I’ve ever made in my life,” he says. Her death also determined the future of the butcher shop.
« C’était elle qui allait poursuivre la: “She was the one who was going to carry on running the shop,” José explains. “She worked a lot with us, she got along with everyone.” Clearly, such a blow of fate affects the entire family structure. “My wife and I threw ourselves into work. I think it was our therapy. Her siblings haven’t recovered yet,” he says.
À l’époque, ils ont eu l’idée de vendre: At the time, they thought about selling the butcher shop and going back to Chile. “We wanted to end everything, but we gradually got back into the routine,” he says. They had just bought an apartment in Chile, which they decided to keep, and that also helped them hold on. But everything had been shattered.
Aujourd’hui, José a 66 ans. « J’ai l’int: Today, José is 66. “I intend to retire any day now, and the butcher shop will end with me,” he says. He looks strong and full of life, but he feels his work takes up a great deal of his time. “You have to be available seven days a week and that comes at a high price: neglecting your family,” he adds. Paradoxically, he is also, in a way, in the service of an extended family made up of his loyal customers. “I think that’s what I’ll miss: the people who come in, who chat, who tell me about their lives.”
Aujourd’hui, cependant, c’est le temps p: Today, however, it is time spent with his family that holds the most important place in his life. José wants to devote more time to his children, who have started their own families with partners they met here, as well as to his five grandchildren, the oldest of whom is now 22 and the youngest barely a year and a half. “I speak to them in Spanish, but they don’t understand me,” he says with a hint of resignation.
José appartient à deux pays et compte bi: José belongs to two countries and fully intends to keep alternating between Chilean and Montréal periods, where his Sundays are sacred, where he gets together with his family and, of course, where he savours his favourite meat: a nice grilled vacío, served with pasta and a big salad.
